sources.title: Unangax̂ History and Culture
sources.annotation: Illustrated historical introduction to houses, seasonal camps, maritime harvesting, kayaks and grass basketry. Pair its generalized descriptions with the named community programs below; they are not a statement that every family followed identical practices.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual HTML introduction, homes, hunting/gathering, transportation, tools and clothes sections read. Population-loss estimates, sensitive ritual detail and linked archaeological-site pages not used. A later automated follow-up timed out after the successful content read.

sections.title: Names, dialects and distinct neighboring peoples
sections.text: Unangam Tunuu is the language name. The university introduction distinguishes Eastern and Western dialects and explains Unangan and Unangas as plural forms, alongside singular Unangax̂. Older Russian use of Aleut covered more than one Alaska Native people. Unangax̂ and Alutiiq/Sugpiaq should therefore remain distinct directory entries; a shared colonial label does not make their languages or governments interchangeable.

sections.title: Maritime knowledge and material life
sections.text: The NPS introduction describes ulax̂ houses built partly into the ground and seasonal camps supporting harvesting. Skin-covered iqyax̂ kayaks joined carefully fitted frames with waterproof sewing. Animal materials supplied food, clothing, tools and containers; grass weaving produced baskets. These are historical technologies requiring skill and environmental knowledge. The contemporary teaching accounts below help connect this material history with continuing cultural learning.

sections.title: Literacy as collaborative work
sections.text: The university traces writing and teaching materials through work involving Unangax̂ speakers, including William Dirks Sr. and Moses Dirks, alongside linguists. Its CoLang 2016 examples describe reuse of earlier learning materials. This introduction is a route into that history; the linked dictionaries, grammars and digital tools have not all been reviewed here.

sections.title: Teacher preparation and community direction
sections.text: APIA describes lesson creation, learning from speakers, intensives and oral proficiency assessment. Its 2019 grant sought a regional teacher-certification pilot; a target of additional teachers is not a measured outcome. Elders, speakers and community members selected through tribal councils advise regional language work. The page also describes Eastern and Atka classes, but its undated timetable is not presented here as a verified current schedule.

sections.title: Using archives with their limits in view
sections.text: The university archive guide identifies linguistic and educational collections, including materials concerning the Commander Islands. Its finding aid can guide further investigation, but a collection description is not inspection of every item. Reproduction and use restrictions apply to some material; linked records and recordings need their own contextual review.

researchGaps: Language-program outcomes, present speaker numbers and the functionality of linked learning tools were not evaluated.
Commander Islands and Russian-language community accounts need direct inspection; the finding aid alone does not establish contemporary conditions.
Historical material-life summaries need more community-specific archaeological and maker perspectives.
